title: ObservabilityCON 2026: A guide to all the announcements from Grafana Labs
description: Today at ObservabilityCON 2026 in San Francisco, we unveiled a range of new Grafana Cloud capabilities designed to reshape cloud economics, bring richer context and deeper visibility across your systems and end-user experiences, and help teams move toward autonomous operations.Check out the keynote to learn more about the latest updates to the open agentic observability cloud, and read on for a quick recap of all the news from ObservabilityCON 2026.Autonomous operations with the help of AIWith Grafana Assistant in Grafana Cloud, you can bring more of your operational tasks together in one place so you can resolve incidents faster and get back to building. And you're doing it with AI features that automate much of the undifferentiated heavy lifting while still keeping you in control. Assistant Investigations, generally available since late July, lets you run longer, deeper investigations that can start automatically from an alert or incident, and teams can run them from the platform, Slack, the Grafana Cloud MCP server, or gcx. And today we're adding new AI features to help you take your automation even further:Assistant Watchers (now generally available) are always-on agents that detect changes not captured by predefined alert rules. You describe what to monitor in plain language and select the relevant data sources. Your watcher then establishes a baseline from historical telemetry patterns and surfaces findings when those patterns change. Grafana Managed Sandboxes (public preview) gives you a controlled cloud environment to ask questions about source code, make changes, and prepare pull requests from conversations in Grafana Cloud. It uses context from your repository code and live telemetry to propose potential fixes within a sandbox environment that a person on your team can then review and approve. Grafana Pages (public preview) lets you build visualizations beyond any fixed constraints, making them closer to an app than a dashboard. You describe what you need, and Assistant builds a page in the canvas—all without you having to write any code. Existing visualization components still work, and Pages supplement them as the next evolution of Grafana. With Grafana Cloud, you decide which parts of your operations you want to handle manually and which parts you want to hand off to Assistant.To learn more about how you can get the most out of Grafana Cloud's AI capabilities, check out our blog posts on autonomous operations and Pages.Cloud economics reimagined  In the AI era, where teams are managing more telemetry than ever, they need to be able to find the right log line in seconds. They also need to know they're only storing the telemetry that's worth paying for. That's why we're making major query performance enhancements to Grafana Cloud Logs, built on technology from our Logline acquisition, and giving you more precision with Adaptive Telemetry, so your costs scale with the value you get from your data.Keep only the data worth paying for: Adaptive Telemetry updatesGrafana Labs’ Adaptive Telemetry suite optimizes cost across metrics, logs, traces, and profiles by recommending what to aggregate or sample, so teams keep the telemetry that matters. Customers have cut telemetry spend by 30% to 50% on average. “Moving to Grafana Cloud and using Adaptive Telemetry cut our metrics costs enough to fund logs and traces as well," says Carl Eastman, Principal Software Engineer, Rapid7. "Our visibility went up while our costs went down, and dashboards and queries are faster and less noisy.” New updates cover logs, metrics, and traces:Adaptive Metrics auto-apply (generally available) continuously applies recommendations, while existing dashboards and alerts keep working unchanged. With cost-first mode, a built-in safeguard only applies recommendations that won’t increase your total active series, so optimization never turns into a cost spike.Adaptive Logs Archive (public preview) routes logs to an object storage bucket you own. Get the cost savings from not putting those logs in Grafana Cloud, but make sure they still exist in low-cost storage for investigations, audits, or compliance requests. And with Adaptive Logs replay (sign up for the private preview), you can bring those logs back on demand.Query traces dropped by Adaptive Traces (generally available) to sample aggressively without worrying about losing the one trace you need. Retrieve any trace by ID from the last 24 hours, even if Adaptive Traces dropped it, so cost savings never come at the expense of an investigation.Volumetric sampling (generally available) gives you a more valuable sample than probabilistic sampling. It spreads your sampling budget fairly across services and request types, so low-volume services aren't crowded out. It also adjusts as your traffic changes. In early testing, it has delivered about 25% higher information density than probabilistic sampling at the same volume.Diversity sampling (generally available) stores a unique combination of attributes such as service, route, and status codes every 15 minutes. When your environment changes, you don't have to write and update custom sampling logic to catch a new service or code path.To learn more, check out our Adaptive Telemetry blog post. Find the log line that matters faster: Full-text search in Grafana Cloud LogsBuilt on technology from Logline, which Grafana Labs acquired in April 2026, Cloud Logs customers are gaining access to faster needle-in-a-haystack queries, at no additional cost. This full-text search capability, now generally available, helps teams find specific log lines, such as those containing request IDs or customer IDs, without scanning massive volumes of data. Faster queries can also benefit AI-driven investigations, where agents execute a large number of queries to help find root causes.“When I ran our first query on newly submitted logs after enabling Logline, the improvement was clear,” said Timo Kirzdörfer, OpenTelemetry & Grafana Cloud Admin, DATEV eG. “We went from processing nearly a terabyte of logs in three minutes to around 100 gigabytes in under three seconds. That represents an 80-90% reduction in the volume of logs searched for newly submitted logs, and we saw the results immediately.” To learn more about full-text search, please visit our docs. Context is king As your systems grow more complex, you and your AI agents need a clearer picture of system health, user experiences, and what needs attention. Our latest Grafana Cloud updates bring more of that context together, expand visibility into the end-user experience, and help streamline everyday workflows.Full-stack observability: more connections, richer context with the Knowledge GraphMost teams have telemetry from across their stack, but connecting those signals to understand what's happening and how it affects users isn't always easy. That’s why we're rolling out new capabilities to advance full-stack observability across Grafana Cloud. With expanded Knowledge Graph coverage and richer operational context, people and AI agents can better understand how systems fit together to investigate issues and find root causes faster.A more connected view of your stackThe Knowledge Graph is the runtime context layer in Grafana Cloud that brings together your system's components, their relationships, and health insights in one connected view.We're evolving the Knowledge Graph to be a platform capability, available in every stack, where you can curate context across Grafana Cloud. We’re also extending the full-stack picture, bringing more of your environment into the Knowledge Graph:Frontend apps (generally available): Frontend Observability maps frontend apps and user-facing signals to the services and infrastructure behind them.Synthetic checks (public preview): Alerts from Synthetic Monitoring checks now appear alongside service health, so you can spot issues and investigate faster.Additional Google Cloud, Azure, and AWS resources (generally available): Cloud Provider Observability now maps more of your Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure resources for a more complete picture of your cloud infrastructure.AI agents (public preview): Agent Observability maps your AI agents alongside their dependencies, so you can see how they connect to the rest of your system.Microsoft SQL Server databases (private preview): Database Observability now discovers SQL Server databases and maps them automatically.Together, these updates help teams investigate issues across more of their stack, from the user experience for their frontend apps to the services, databases, and infrastructure supporting it.More operational context for people and AI agentsKnowing how your system fits together is important, but to investigate issues effectively, you also need context that’s unique to your organization, including which teams are responsible for which services and what you've learned from past incidents.We're bringing more of that context into the Knowledge Graph, and making it available to both engineering teams and the AI agents they work with every day:Service ownership (private preview): An integration with Grafana Cloud Service Center connects services to the teams who own them, on-call schedules, and runbooks, so following a dependency also shows who can act on it.Custom entities and relationships (generally available): Define and map custom entities and relationships that are specific to your organization's products, business processes, and more. Use Knowledge Graph mode in Grafana Assistant to help configure these connections.Operational context from past incidents (private preview): An integration with Grafana Cloud IRM connects actions and outcomes from previous investigations to relevant parts of your system, so you can build on what you’ve already learned.The Knowledge Graph is also available as runtime context for AI agents (generally available). Whether you're using Grafana Assistant or bringing your own agent through gcx, this lets you and your agents work from the same shared context.For a deeper dive on these new features, check out our full-stack observability blog post.Digital Experience Monitoring: see where users struggle, not just when systems failHealthy systems don't always mean happy users. To understand how your applications are really performing, you need visibility into the end-user experience.In Grafana Cloud, we've been building that foundation for Digital Experience Monitoring by bringing together Synthetic Monitoring and Frontend Observability, connecting proactive testing with real user signals. Together, they help teams understand not just whether an application is working as expected, but how it's actually performing for users.At ObservabilityCON, we’re spotlighting new features to further build out Digital Experience Monitoring with Grafana Cloud, so you can further close the gap between system health and user experiences:Session Replay (public preview): Watch a recording of what your users actually did in your application. Correlate when something breaks to the underlying telemetry so that you know exactly what happened. Mobile Observability  (private preview): Extend Frontend Observability to your iOS, Android, React Native, and Flutter apps using upstream native OpenTelemetry SDKs. See what mobile users experience, and connect it to the same telemetry as the rest of your stack.Critical User Journeys (private preview): Define which journeys matter most, so every team works from the same definition of “critical” instead of improvising its own. Explore a journey end to end and go from a drop in conversion rate to the root cause in a single view.You can learn more about Digital Experience Monitoring with Grafana Cloud here, and get started today by signing up for the Grafana Cloud free tier today.Grafana Workflows: turn processes into automated stepsCoordinating an incident response can be so time-consuming that it pulls you away from actually understanding and fixing the problem. But with Grafana Workflows (public preview), you can focus on what really matters by turning your team’s processes into automated steps.Grafana Workflows gives you event-driven automation that connects actions across Grafana Cloud and your other tools, with Grafana Assistant available for steps that need analysis or writing. Prebuilt blueprints cover major incident kickoff, on-call handoff reports, and weekly service health summaries.For example, a workflow can create an incident channel, page support according to your team’s rules, and ask Assistant to prepare a briefing from the available evidence. And once you define the workflow, Grafana Cloud can prepare the next engineer's handoff or gather the findings for your weekly service review. You decide what should happen consistently and where AI can help make sense of changing information.Expand what’s possible with Grafana: the Grafana Marketplace is generally available The Grafana Marketplace is now generally available, giving teams more ways to extend Grafana with specialized, partner-built plugins. Since launching as a pilot program earlier this year, the Marketplace has grown to include more than 30 plugins spanning security, networking, cloud cost optimization, and more. These paid plugins come with partner-backed commitments to ongoing maintenance, compatibility, and support, helping users confidently connect Grafana to the specialized tools they rely on everyday. Grafana Cloud users can now try Marketplace plugins free for 14 days, with full functionality throughout the trial. Learn more in our blog post, and start exploring the Marketplace today. Check out the ObservabilityCON 2026 homepage for all the latest updates from Grafana Labs' flagships observability event!

title: From production problem to proposed fix: Implement autonomous operations with Grafana AI
description: You've just finished a deployment, and though your service is up, you start to notice some requests are getting slower. To address the lag, someone—or, more likely, some group of people on your team—needs to watch the dashboards, decide whether the change matters, investigate what happened, and turn the findings into a fix. At each step you're gathering context—and often explaining that context again to the next person or tool. To make matters worse for the team responsible for the service, all this work is getting in the way of everything else they need to build. With Grafana Assistant in Grafana Cloud, you can bring more of those tasks together in one place, helping you resolve incidents faster so you can get back to building. And you're doing it with AI features that automate much of the undifferentiated heavy lifting while still keeping you in control. Assistant Watchers (generally available today as part of ObservabilityCON 2026) provides ongoing attention to the conditions you care about. Assistant Investigations (generally available) gathers evidence about what changed. And Grafana Managed Sandboxes (public preview as of today) uses that context to prepare changes in a controlled cloud environment, giving your team something concrete to review. In this blog post, I'll show you how you can use these features collectively for better observability outcomes.Give the service ongoing attentionConsider a checkout service after a release. You want to know whether customers are encountering sustained errors or slower responses, while also accounting for the brief disruption you expect during deployment. With Watchers, our always-on agents, you describe that concern and select the relevant data sources. Assistant then analyzes your historical telemetry to establish a baseline and calibrate the checks. From there, the watcher periodically assesses those signals and provides reporting along with the evidence behind its findings. If a watcher finds a critical issue, it can automatically start an investigation with Investigations, our agent designed to help you go really deep into your incidents. That way, you can delegate recurring health checks to Assistant so your team can focus on other tasks instead. Existing alerts continue to cover known conditions that require dependable paging, while the watcher adds contextual assessment around the service. The best part: With support for Google BigQuery alongside operational telemetry sources, your watchers aren't limited to traditional observability scenarios. They can also monitor business signals, helping your entire organization keep tabs on critical changes that could impact the bottom line.Start investigating with the evidence attachedOf course, a notification is just the beginning of the response. The next questions are familiar: Which requests are affected? When did the behavior change? Is the database involved, or is another dependency slowing down?Investigations can explore metrics, logs, traces, and profiles, test hypotheses, and assemble findings with supporting source queries. From there, your responders can inspect the evidence and steer the investigation as they learn more.In our checkout example, suppose the evidence points toward repeated database calls in a request path. The useful handoff to a developer now includes the affected service, the symptoms, and the evidence supporting that hypothesis. The user has a starting point for checking the code.Turn the findings into a proposed changeManaged Sandboxes, which give Assistant a controlled cloud environment to develop proposed fixes using repository code and live telemetry, carry that investigation context into your codebase. With the relevant repository connected and coding enabled, an agent can inspect the code, prepare changes, and run available checks in a Grafana sandbox.For our example, the task could be to examine the database access pattern, prepare a targeted change, and add a regression test. Managed Sandboxes' repository-specific environments can provide the tools and dependencies needed to build and test the project. The goal should be for Assistant to deliver a proposed pull request that the team can evaluate: what changed, why it addresses the suspected cause, which checks ran, and what still needs verification. So when you respond, the investigation is already underway, with supporting telemetry and, as the workflow progresses, a proposed fix to review.Keep the decisions visible, and stay in controlA passing test is useful evidence, but your team still needs to confirm recovery in production as part of its release process. Your reviewers need to decide whether the diagnosis fits, whether the proposed change is appropriate, and how to deploy it. After rollout, they can use production telemetry to check the outcome and keep monitoring for recurrence.That makes autonomy practical: delegate recurring observation, evidence gathering, and preparation of changes, while retaining clear decisions about what reaches production. You decide which parts you want to inspect, whether it's with Managed Sandboxes, Assistant Automations (to run recurring tasks), or Watchers. For some tasks, you might opt to hand it off to Assistant completely.It also creates a useful way to judge the workflow. Did your responder spend less time gathering context? Did the developer receive enough evidence to act? Was the proposed change easier to review?Start with one service, then scaleYou can implement a similar level of automation with Assistant today. To start, choose a service your team already watches manually after releases. Define the behavior that matters, calibrate a watcher, and review its findings. Configure investigation escalations where appropriate.Then, where Managed Sandboxes are enabled, connect a relevant repository and try a bounded task with a clear review outcome. Start with a problem your team understands. Use each run to improve the checks, context, and verification. Expand the work you delegate as the results earn your confidence.After you collected some experiences and found the mode you want to work in, you can scale this to your liking. Assistant features are all interoperable; you can use Automations to set up Managed Sandboxes or Investigations, chat in Slack about the results of the latest incidents, and analyze all your alerts in the last 30 days periodically to improve the ones that don’t perform.We’re excited to see what you can automate to help improve your operations.

title: Grafana Pages: Turn data into interactive experiences with the next evolution of Grafana
description: Teams often spend as much time preparing information as discussing it: gathering charts, checking business reports, and finding the GitHub activity that explains a change. Every follow-up question can lead to yet another round of work. That's why, as part of ObservabilityCON 2026, we're excited to introduce Grafana Pages, a new feature in Grafana Cloud that gives you a canvas to describe what you need and build a live app in minutes, based on your real data, context, and interactions. From new types of visualizations to slides and even to games, the only limitation is your imagination.With Pages, currently in public preview, you can create interactive views and tools with Grafana Assistant, using the data you already access through Grafana. There's no code and no setup; no export, upload, or deploy steps. Unlike standard dashboards, which are fixed grids of panels, you simply describe what you need, refine it through conversation, and share it with your team to explore and return to as needed.What Pages unlocksPages let you build trusted, reliable, and scalable (mini) apps in the environment you know and use with Grafana Assistant by your side. Oftentimes, broad solutions might miss a use case that’s specific to your organization. But with Pages you can easily build and own your own information hub, whether it's an incident view, a runbook, a deploy tracker, an exec readout, or a customer-facing status page.Let's look at some ways you can build Pages today.Build on your existing data connectionsGetting an internal tool working starts with connecting it to useful data. Pages builds on the data connections you already use in Grafana, giving you a starting point for bringing operational and business information together.Put transaction volumes beside service performance, or build a release review around production trends and relevant connected context. Spend your effort shaping the experience around the question your team needs to answer, rather than getting bogged down trying to figure out all the visualization bells and whistles.Let colleagues answer the next questionA shared view often leads to other questions you hadn't initially considered. One person might want to know about impacts on a specific region. A second might ask when the issue started, while a third wants to know which service is driving the change.Pages can include filters, time-range controls, and drilldowns so colleagues can explore those questions themselves. Start with an overview, narrow it to a region or service, and inspect the supporting detail—all without asking someone to prepare another report.Reuse the work; take the idea furtherBuild a page once, then return to it with a new time range for the next review. Refine it through Assistant as your team discovers which comparisons and details matter.The remix feature in Pages gives a good idea room to grow. A colleague might build a useful deployment tracker; you might see how to extend it into a broader release review. Start from their Page, add your perspective, and turn it into something neither of you had to build from scratch.Trust what you seeA page is only useful if people believe it. Every page keeps its sources, which are the queries behind each chart and number, so you and your colleagues can check where a value came from instead of taking Assistant's word for it. To validate a page you've built, open a source in Explore mode in Grafana Cloud to run the same query over the same time range, compare it with what the Page shows, and keep digging from there.Pages also build on the access you already have. They work with any existing data connections you have configured in Grafana Cloud, and Grafana's permissions and data source policies still apply to every request. If a page can do something beyond reading data, like sending a Slack message or making an HTTP request, Grafana shows you the destination and values to review before it runs.See what people are buildingEarly internal examples show the range of experiences people are creating with Pages, from business monitoring to release tools and visual storytelling. In this section, we'll link to some of these projects so you can check them out. We've also embedded several of the pages directly into this post so you can interact with them here, too.Run your operationsPages can replace the tab-hopping that comes with triage, audits, and capacity reviews. Each of these examples gathers the data, ranks what matters, and lets you act on it.Triage. Check the health of services across the (fictional) Astronomy Shop and Bank production namespaces. Triage surfaces SLO burn, error and latency regressions, and firing alerts. Pick the most urgent service and open an investigation from the same view.Service health. See which services are burning or have spent their SLO error budget. Select a service to drill into its traffic, error rate, p95 latency, and firing alerts over the time range you choose.Rightsizing. Compare Kubernetes CPU and memory requests against actual usage. Find workloads that are overprovisioned or starved, see the monthly cost of fixing them, and build a patch bundle of recommended request changes.Alert Noise Audit. Find which alert rules produce the noisiest firing episodes. Classify them as flapping, always firing, broken, or night pager. Review fixes such as pending periods or keep-firing-for settings before you apply them.Explore your dataA page can turn a data source into something you want to look at and click through, not only read.Observatory. Request rates, error ratios, latency, service call paths, and recent orders for the Astronomy Shop appear as an interactive star map. The busiest services glow brightest, failing calls stand out, and you can follow a single order across the sky.The Restless Planet. Recent USGS earthquake activity becomes a scrolling story for any time window you choose. It shows how often quakes occurred, where they clustered, and how their energy was distributed. Change the window and every sentence recalculates.Tell the storyPages aren't limited to dashboards. Use them to present results, because the numbers stay live while the format changes.Week in Review. A weekly review of Astronomy Shop and Bank service health, SLOs, alerts, latency, cost, and customers. It's a navigable slide deck with presenter notes, ready for a Monday meeting.Stack Wrapped. A story-style recap of your stack's week, covering requests, latency, alerts, SLO performance, regional revenue, and cluster cost. It's built to be shared, with tap-through cards.Just for funTail Run. Fly a game-style run through one minute-by-minute stretch of a production service's latency and error data. p99 latency sets the ceiling, and error rate and median latency set the floor. You can see how the service behaved while you play.Start with one question your team keeps askingYou can start building Pages today. We suggest you choose a recurring task that sends someone across dashboards, reports, or connected tools. Identify who needs the result and what they should be able to explore. Then describe that to Assistant, using the sources you have connected.For example, try this prompt in Assistant:Create a store operations page using our transaction and payment-error data. Let me compare regions, select a store, and change the time range. Show missing data clearly and include links to the sources.Try the first version, check representative values against the source, and refine the controls with the people who will use them. A useful next request might be: “Add a comparison with the previous week and put payment errors beside the transaction trend.”You can even turn your most viewed dashboard into a page and see what it looks like with filters and drilldowns added.Either way, start with something that saves your team one repeated round of preparation. Create a page and keep improving it as the questions change. Your first draft takes just a few minutes, from there on you can plan longer or shorter iterations and refinements.And if you aren't already using Grafana Cloud, you can sign up for our forever-free tier and test Pages there, too!

title: Break the link between data volume and your observability bill with Adaptive Telemetry
description: In the AI era, where telemetry is generated by every model call, tool invocation, and agent step, organizations need more help than ever when it comes to navigating the economics of observability.For a lot of teams, the default response is a "data diet" of shorter retention, which leaves services or environments out of collection, or basic sampling, which is more guesswork than strategy. Either way, you end up cutting to control the bill, and you risk losing the very data you need during an incident.Your costs shouldn't scale with how much data you ingest. Instead, they should scale with the value you get from it, so you only pay to keep the data that earns its place.That’s what Adaptive Telemetry is built for, and organizations such as Rapid7 are already seeing the results.“Moving to Grafana Cloud and using Adaptive Telemetry cut our metrics costs enough to fund logs and traces as well," says Carl Eastman, Principal Software Engineer, Rapid7. "Our visibility went up while our costs went down, and dashboards and queries are faster and less noisy.” You can already use Adaptive Telemetry for all your observability signals, and we're continuing to build on that foundation so you can get even more precise about which traces you keep, improve your logs economics, and get more from Adaptive Metrics with less toil. Here's how that looks in practice.Keep only the traces that matter, and cut volume by 90% Traces are where the data diet hurts most. Many teams sample with a fixed percentage, which treats a slow checkout request the same as a routine health check. Cut the percentage and your bill drops, but so does the chance that the trace you need is still there when something breaks.Adaptive Traces already handles the hard part (tail sampling) without you running a pipeline. Three newer capabilities make retention even more precise.Automatically keep your most valuable traces, without the policy toilVolumetric sampling gives you a more valuable sample than probabilistic sampling does. It spreads your sampling budget fairly across services and request types, so low-volume services aren't crowded out, and it keeps adjusting as your traffic changes. You set one number (your sampling percentage) without writing complicated policies or tuning them by hand. In Grafana Labs' testing, it delivered about 25% higher information density than probabilistic sampling at the same volume.Keep at least one trace from each footprint, so there’s always something to reference Diversity sampling makes sure you always have something to look at. Every 15 minutes, it stores a unique combination of attributes such as service, route, and status codes. When your environment changes, you don't have to write and update custom sampling logic to catch a new service or code path.Sample aggressively and still retrieve the exact trace you need The ability to query traces dropped by Adaptive Traces is your safety net. Adaptive Traces keeps every dropped trace queryable by trace ID for 24 hours after ingest. If you have the trace ID from a log line, a support ticket, or a testing framework, you can retrieve that specific trace even if Adaptive Traces dropped it. Dropped traces don't appear in search or aggregations, so it's a lookup, not a replacement for sampling the traces you want to search. That's what lets you sample aggressively with confidence.Together, you can use these features to cut trace volume significantly without wondering whether you cut something you needed.Volumetric and diversity sampling, along with the ability to query dropped traces, are all generally available.Improve your logs economics without giving up the data you might needLogs add up fast, and a lot of what you store never gets looked at. Adaptive Logs already finds the log patterns nobody queries and trims them on the way in. Now, two new capabilities help you cut earlier, and with more confidence.Drop unwanted logs at the source and cut egress and network overheadFleet-managed Adaptive Logs uses the same drop rules and exemptions you already use and applies them directly to the collectors you already run, through Fleet Management. Matching logs are filtered out before they ever leave your environment, so you save on egress and network overhead on top of your storage savings. Adaptive Logs creates and keeps the collector pipelines in sync for you, so there's nothing extra to write or maintain. Pattern-based recommendations still run in Grafana Cloud for everything that remains.Keep what you might need, retain it in low-cost storageTeams are understandably cautious about dropping logs. After all, a dropped line can't be recovered, so it's understandable when teams hold back. Archive and replay changes that. Archive routes logs to your own low-cost object storage instead of dropping them. Replay brings them back on demand when you need them for an investigation, an audit, or a compliance request. You keep the savings from not indexing low-value logs, without permanently losing data you might need later.That's the shift: lower costs, with a way back to the data you might need.Fleet-managed Adaptive Logs is in public preview. Archive is in public preview, and replay is coming soon. Sign up for the private preview to get early access. Get more from Adaptive Metrics, with less toilAdaptive Metrics is already good at finding the waste. It looks at how your metrics are actually used across dashboards, alerts, recording rules and queries, and it recommends aggregating the ones nobody needs at full detail into lower-cardinality versions. The catch is that someone has to review each recommendation, and for platform teams, that review quickly becomes its own chore. Rapid7's Eastman knows the feeling:“Before, finding waste meant someone manually digging through metric cardinality and log volume, and the job never ended because new services kept adding more," Eastman said. "Adaptive Metrics and Adaptive Logs now do that analysis for us... Our engineers spend their time on the few rules that need human judgment... rather than the whole long tail.”Apply savings automatically, without reviewing every recommendation Auto-Apply takes the review off your plate. Turn it on for a segment, and new recommendations are applied automatically as they're generated, with no human in the loop.You choose where it runs, and you can exempt the metrics you never want touched. Use coverage-first mode to keep pace with usage automatically, or cost-first mode if you’d rather guarantee your series count never increasesAuto-Apply is generally available. For the full walkthrough, see our recent blog post on the topic.Ready for the next wave of telemetryAI will bring more telemetry, but it doesn't have to bring more cost and more noise with it. Trim what nobody uses, keep the signals that matter, and know the data you might need isn't lost for good. You don't have to cut retention, leave services out of collection, or sample on a hunch.That matters beyond the bill. When your costs follow the value of your data, the savings are yours to reinvest in broader coverage and better insight, instead of living on a data diet. Rapid7 is a good example. Here’s how they describe it: “We’re reinvesting the savings in observability coverage rather than just banking them," Eastman said. "Every signal has to earn its place, and the savings pay for signals that do.” Whether it's metrics, logs, traces, or profiles, Adaptive Telemetry helps you keep what's valuable as your data grows.Adaptive Telemetry is available in Grafana Cloud. Try it today, and read our docs to learn more!

title: Full-stack observability in Grafana Cloud: More connections, richer context, and faster investigations for users and agents
description: Most teams have telemetry from across their stack, but connecting those signals to understand what's happening and how it affects users isn't always easy. Critical context about service dependencies, ownership, and past incidents often lives across tools, runbooks, and conversations between team members.That’s why, today at ObservabilityCON 2026, we’re announcing new capabilities that advance full-stack observability across Grafana Cloud. Powering this experience is the Knowledge Graph, the runtime context layer in Grafana Cloud that brings together your system's components, their relationships, and health insights in one connected view.We're expanding the Knowledge Graph to cover more infrastructure, applications, and user-facing signals, along with a broader range of operational context, including your service catalog, the teams on call, and lessons captured during past incidents. Together, these connections give people and AI agents the same shared context, built on open standards, about how a system fits together, helping them to troubleshoot and find root causes faster. “We've found that the hardest part of an investigation is rarely a lack of data. The challenge is connecting service ownership, dependencies, operational knowledge, and customer impact across a complex ecosystem,” said Neil Wilson, Senior Director of Software Engineering at LexisNexis Risk Solutions. “Entity graph relationships [on the Knowledge Graph] help make those connections visible, giving engineers and AI systems the context they need to move from data to understanding to action."Think of Grafana Cloud as your SRE specialist: whether you work with Grafana Assistant or bring your own agent through gcx, you want that specialized expertise available when you need it, without spending the first half of an investigation reconstructing how everything fits together. That's where we're taking full-stack observability: towards faster, more reliable, and more cost-effective answers, powered by the Knowledge Graph.A connected view of your system: making the full stack even fullerWe're evolving the Knowledge Graph to be a platform capability, available in every stack, where you can curate context across Grafana Cloud.Traditionally, the Knowledge Graph has supported Grafana Cloud Application Observability, Kubernetes Monitoring, Database Observability, and Cloud Provider Observability. These solutions automatically discover their respective entities, such as services, pods, and nodes, and map these entities and their relationships onto the Knowledge Graph. They then monitor entity health and add these insights onto the graph, highlighting everything from deviations from dynamic baselines to configuration changes.Now we're extending that full-stack picture, bringing more of your environment into the Knowledge Graph:Frontend apps (generally available): Frontend Observability maps frontend apps and user-facing signals to the services and infrastructure behind them.Synthetic checks (public preview): Alerts from Synthetic Monitoring checks now appear alongside service health, so you can spot issues and investigate faster.More Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure cloud resources (generally available): Cloud Provider Observability now maps more of your Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure resources for a more complete picture of your cloud infrastructure.AI agents (public preview): Agent Observability maps your AI agents alongside their dependencies, so you can see how they connect to the rest of your system.Microsoft SQL Server databases (private preview): Database Observability now discovers SQL Server databases and maps them automatically.With these updates, you can investigate issues across more of your stack, from a user-facing app to the services, databases, and infrastructure behind it.Go beyond telemetry with richer context in the Knowledge Graph Knowing how your system fits together is important, but to investigate issues effectively, you also need context that’s unique to your organization, including which teams are responsible for which services, how those services support your products and business processes, and what you've learned from past incidents.We're bringing more of that context into the Knowledge Graph, and making it available to both engineering teams and the AI agents they work with every day. Service context: connect services to their owners with Grafana Cloud Service CenterWhile your telemetry describes what’s actually running, a service catalog describes your system in terms your organization understands. Connecting the two gives an investigation a route from a deployed component to the service it belongs to, the team responsible for it, and the guidance they maintain.The new Knowledge Graph integration with Grafana Cloud Service Center, now in private preview, brings these connections onto the graph, so you can see service ownership, on-call schedules, and runbooks alongside the components they support.For example, let’s take Everyday Checking, an imaginary banking app powered by account management and card payments services. If account creation slows down, you need to know which deployment is affected, which team owns it, who’s on call, and where to find the account creation runbook. Having all that information connected in the Knowledge Graph gives an engineer or an agent a much more useful place to start.Team context: add custom entities with Grafana Assistant Your team knows things that no automatic discovery process can infer. Account management and card payments might belong to the Everyday Checking app. A group of services might support a specific online product or business process. You should be able to make those relationships available to everyone in your org via the Knowledge Graph.That’s why we built custom entities and relationships, now generally available. They let you define rules based on your telemetry to create the entities you need, connect them to the rest of the Knowledge Graph, and attach health insights. For example, if multiple services share the label product_line="everyday-checking", you can use that label to group them under a new Everyday Checking product entity.You can also use Knowledge Graph mode in Grafana Assistant, now generally available, to help define these custom entities and relationships. Ask how to model your product, write a custom rule, or investigate a missing connection, and Assistant can guide you through the process.Operational context: give the next investigation the benefit of the lastSome of your most useful operational knowledge is created when something goes wrong: someone tests a hypothesis and rules it out; a restart appears to help, but the errors return; a configuration change finally restores service. By the end of the investigation, the team has learned far more than the final root cause.Through an integration with Grafana Cloud IRM, we’re bringing those lessons onto the Knowledge Graph as operational context, now in private preview. This goes beyond attaching an incident summary to a service. We’re extracting hypotheses, actions, and their outcomes from the evidence captured during investigations, and connecting them to the relevant parts of your system.To revisit our Everyday Checking example, imagine the team tried a restart, saw the errors return, then restored account creation by reverting a database connection pool setting. The next investigation could use that history to check whether the same conditions apply, and whether another restart is worth trying. The earlier incident provides a lead to test against current telemetry.Runtime context: give agents and people the same starting pointEach connection surfaced in the Knowledge Graph makes it possible for teams to ask more useful questions. Which services support this product? Which deployment is affected? Who owns it? What did we try the last time this happened?People can explore those connections in Grafana Cloud. And now, with the Knowledge Graph available as runtime context for AI agents, a capability that’s generally available, Grafana Assistant and your own agents connected through gcx can work from that same shared understanding of your system.“We had a latency alert fire, then a second alert in our downstream HPCC system. The real issue turned out to be a call to an external vendor that exhausted the connection pool at our database layer,” said LexisNexis Solutions’ Wilson. “Assistant walked down the Knowledge Graph and got us to that root cause a lot quicker, and it kept teams off paths they had already started down.” Our new Cypher query tool also lets agents ask the Knowledge Graph direct questions about how your system connects. Cypher is a standard graph query language: you describe a pattern, such as “every service that calls this database and the pods it runs on,” and get back each match with its relationships and current health. This helps agents build on context already available to them rather than reconstruct from raw telemetry each time. Get started todayWith more of your system and operational knowledge connected through the Knowledge Graph, you and your AI agents have a clearer picture of how everything fits together. That means you can spend less time piecing together context and find root cause faster.Ready to get started? Ask Grafana Assistant: “How can I get more from my Knowledge Graph?” and get specific recommendations based on your stack. Note: some changes may require admin access.You can also fill out this form to access the private previews mentioned throughout this post, including mapping Microsoft SQL Server databases to the Knowledge Graph, and learn more in our Knowledge Graph documentation.

title: Expand what’s possible with Grafana: The Grafana Marketplace is now generally available
description: Earlier this year, we launched the Grafana Marketplace, a platform that gives independent software vendors, systems integrators, and developers in the Grafana community a new way to sell and distribute plugins built for Grafana.The Marketplace builds on our existing plugin catalog by enabling third-party partners and developers to earn revenue from their plugins and invest further in their development. For end users, these paid Marketplace plugins come with guarantees for ongoing updates and support, helping ensure the integrations you rely on remain secure and reliable over time.Since launching the pilot program in April, the Marketplace has grown to include more than 30 custom, partner-backed plugins for high-demand data sources and apps, ranging from cloud cost optimization tools to security solutions from Rubrik and Cisco. Today at ObservabilityCON 2026, we’re excited to share that the Grafana Marketplace is generally available. And to make it easier to explore, any Grafana Cloud user can now trial Marketplace plugins free for 14 days.Why the Marketplace mattersThe Grafana plugin catalog includes more than 300 plugins built and maintained by Grafana Labs, our partners, and the community. This ecosystem gives users more ways to connect Grafana to the tools and data sources they rely on, while giving developers the freedom to extend Grafana for new use cases.We want developers to be inspired to keep building on Grafana, while our users have more options for monitoring their infrastructure and managing their Grafana instances, including apps and data sources for specialized use cases.But building and maintaining a production-grade plugin takes a lot of work. Until recently, independent developers and systems integrators had no direct way to fund that work through the Grafana plugin ecosystem. The Marketplace introduced that commercial model. By giving partners a way to earn revenue from their plugins, they can invest in ongoing development and support while bringing more specialized solutions to Grafana Cloud and Grafana Enterprise users across observability, security, IoT, and beyond. The result is more production-ready data sources and apps reaching the catalog, backed by the ongoing support users need to rely on them.Importantly, the Marketplace adds to our existing plugin ecosystem; it doesn’t replace it. Community and open source plugins remain a core part of Grafana, and developers can continue to build and publish free plugins just as they do today. The Marketplace provides another path for developers who want to sell their plugins and take on the corresponding support and maintenance commitments.Explore the growing Grafana Marketplace Since we launched the pilot, the Marketplace has grown to cover more than 30 high-demand data sources and apps, with options spanning networking, security, storage, virtualization, collaboration, cost management, industrial infrastructure, and more.Below are some examples of the Marketplace plugins available today:Network and security: Cisco Meraki, Rubrik Security Cloud, Zscaler ZIA and ZPA, and Akamai data sources from Crest Data.Storage and virtualization: NetApp ONTAP, Dell PowerScale, and VMware vSphere from Crest Data, and Proxmox VE from Ridgeline Technologies.Productivity and collaboration: SharePoint, Citrix Cloud, Tableau, and Zoom from Crest Data, and end-to-end Microsoft Teams observability from Phenisys.Cost and compute: Kubecost and Nutanix from Integration Plumbers.Industrial infrastructure: Helin Connect Data Hub data source from Helin Data.Manufacturing quality analytics: A full statistical process control (SPC) suite and 3D CAD visualization from KensoBI.Marketplace plugins run inside your own Grafana instance, and Grafana Labs reviews every listing before it goes live. All plugins must be cryptographically signed and must encrypt sensitive data. Partners are contractually obligated to remediate critical vulnerabilities within seven days and high-severity vulnerabilities within 30 days.While Grafana Labs handles billing and payment, support for these plugins comes directly from the partners who built them. We vet every partner and each one is contractually committed to keeping its plugins compatible with supported Grafana versions. Try Marketplace plugins free in Grafana CloudEvery Marketplace plugin comes with a 14-day free trial and full functionality from the first click. Find these plugins in the catalog, or in the Plugins tab of your Grafana Cloud stack, and start a trial.If you're a contracted Grafana Cloud customer, please reach out to your account team to set up your trial. We’d love to hear from youThe Grafana Marketplace is still early, and we want to keep building it the Grafana Labs way: with your input. If a technology you rely on isn't covered yet, reach out at plugins-marketplace@grafana.com.  And if you’re a developer interested in contributing your plugins to the Marketplace, please submit this form.

title: Prometheus and OpenTelemetry interoperability in 2026: Survey results
description:
We ran a survey asking users of OpenTelemetry and Prometheus how they collect,
process, and store metrics. The goal was to understand, with real usage data
rather than assumptions, how far the ecosystem has moved and whether the
interoperability still causes friction.
Key takeaways

Interoperability has measurably improved since our
2024 survey: the average
ease-of-use rating rose from 3.1 to 3.6, the equivalent of one in two
respondents rating a whole category higher, and the share of respondents
finding the two hard to use together fell from 29% to 10%.
In infrastructure instrumentation, Prometheus exporters remain the most-used
method (72%) with OTel receivers close behind (57%), and nearly half of
respondents run both at once rather than migrating from one to the other.
In application instrumentation, OTel SDKs are the most-used method at 65%
with Prometheus SDKs at 52%, and 41% use only the OTel style of application
instrumentation.
Prometheus relabeling rules (54%) and the open source OTel Collector (53%)
are the two most common processing steps, and 65% of respondents run a
“vanilla stack” of one or both with no vendor transformation or custom
Collector build anywhere in the pipeline.

title: Fragments: October  4
description:
In response to my last fragments (probably the bit about us worrying if LLMs have consciousness when we when we should be wondering why they don’t have a conscience) “Metalanguage” replied:


  we shipped the id and forgot the superego. classic software lifecycle.


I don’t know what was on their mind, but their post immediately made me think of the classic 1956 movie Forbidden Planet. Plenty of sci-fi, and other literature, have explored humans creating technology with unintended behavior, going back at least to Mary Shelly. But that movie was particularly influential on sci-fi film-making and in the heart of its story is what happens when we nurture a thinking machine.

I use the term “nurture” here deliberately. We talk of building software, but building implies a degree of determinism. When we build a bridge, or a locomotive, we expect it to behave in a controlled and well-understood manner. That’s a difference in degree to how we cultivate plants in our garden, or nurture young children. One of the challenges of working with these systems is understanding what has changed in this shift from building a computational system to nurturing an inferential one, and how our processes need to change in response.

We get unintended behavior with deterministic building: some bridges have collapsed, and our  computational systems often have bugs. But one difference is that when we find a bug in a computational system we can usually fix it. Even if we can’t, we can usually disable a component so the bug won’t do further harm. With inferential LLMs however, there is no such simple fix or disablement, which may lead us to the fate of the Krell.

(If you haven’t seen Forbidden Planet, it’s well worth watching. Yes, it shows it was made in the 1950s - with special effects, music, acting, and attitudes of that decade. But the story is solid, and its key theme is very relevant to the future we build with generative AI. Just don’t read about it in advance, it’s better to be immersed in the story without spoilers - although my memory of that experience is understandably hazy.)

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Many people who follow me also know my friend Ola Bini, who was my colleague at Thoughtworks for many years, and was living in Ecuador working as an independent software security expert. Sadly his time in Ecuador was dogged by a bogus prosecution by the authorities there. But things seemed to have settled down, and although not allowed to leave Ecuador, Ola was able to get on with his life.

Sadly that’s no longer the case as he was deported from Ecuador on Friday:


  According to information released by his lawyer, Bini was intercepted by a car with four people who identified themselves as immigration agents. He was then taken to an immigration office without further information or a formal order from a competent authority. There, officials told Bini that his visa had been revoked but didn’t show any supporting document.

  Bini’s defense filed a habeas corpus to safeguard his freedom and prevent his deportation. Yet, Ecuadorian authorities affirmed that the developer represents a threat or risk to public security and the state structure, and must leave the country. The ground for deportation is a secret report which allegedly asserts that Bini committed acts against the security of Ecuador. The defense could not access its contents.


I was really worried for a while, since it wasn’t clear where he was going to be deported to. But he tweeted from Sweden, so I’m thankful for that. But this is only a partial relief. Ola has spent thirteen years in Ecuador and made it his home. To be thrown out of your home for scant reason is a heavy thing to bear, and the officials who did that have committed a serious offense.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

DDD Europe have released the video of Gien Verschatse interviewing Eric Evans and myself at the conference in June. We start by talking about how we bonded over conceptual modeling in the late 1990s. The conversation quickly moves to AI, we note that it’s impossible to predict how such a big change will work out. We do expect that it will cause us to think about our work in different ways, but the change may well be liberating, it’s reinvigorated Eric’s love of programming.


  people are probably going to feel very frustrated by [the new way of thinking about software]… but when you get through that, there is a kind of a wonderful feeling of my brain’s been loosened up.


Our background in agile planning helps with the uncertainty, as we are used to taking small steps and being attentive to feedback. We mull on the interplay of writing and thinking, in terms of both prose and code, and how its very much an iterative process of exploration and refinement - the same is true when we chat with our LLMs.

And don’t miss Eric’s important final tip.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Paul Graham:


  There were a lot of things that only worked because there’s a limit to the rate at which humans can operate. We’re about to find out what all of them are, as they break.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

The speculation continues about whether or not reading code will play a part in a software developer’s future. Geoffrey Huntley says.


  People are still saying, very loudly, that code should be readable so that humans can understand it. I no longer think that’s the goal.


Interestingly his example has the LLM explain a haskell function definition… by translating it to Python. Which, to me, suggests there is a role for code - just that LLM need not store code in the same form that it presents it to a reader. This is essentially the same idea as projectional editing, which posits that the editable representation of software need not be the same as its storage representation.

Sam Ruby touches on this as he muses on a Rails World keynote. He quotes DHH saying:


  Rust is a good prompt compilation target for the moment, but so is C++. And soon assembler. Then microcode. Myopic to think we’re going to stop the agentic drill bit until it reaches computing bedrock.


He responds with:


  The post leaves one question unasked, though: what sits at the top of the drill? What do we keep, edit and trust as the source of truth?


He carries out exercise of looking at some Rails software. Represented in Ruby/Rails and its about 60,000 tokens. Compiling it into C it turns into 4,000,000 tokens. That increase in token size will hamper the LLM, that still has to fit it into its context window, and even if it were to fit, figure out where to focus its attention. Sam points out reasons why, even absent a human reading it, it makes sense to represent the program in a higher-level language.


  what Rails becomes when agents write the code: the most compact, precise and conventional specification of a web application, whatever it ends up compiled to.

  Let the drill go as deep as it can. Just keep the notation at the top.


This all reminds me of what Unmesh Joshi argued: that code serves “two distinct
but intertwined purposes”: instructions to a machine, and a conceptual model of
the problem domain. After exploring how those change with LLMs he concludes:


  The role of coding is not disappearing. But it is changing.

  As LLMs make code generation cheaper, the mechanical act of writing instructions becomes less central. What becomes more important is making the conceptual model explicit, discovering the right vocabulary, and refining that vocabulary through iteration, domain expertise, and feedback. This is also why programming languages continue to matter deeply. We are not meant to be passive reviewers of generated code. The act of writing code is itself part of our thinking.

  Code is still instructions for a machine. But it is also a model of understanding. In the LLM era, that second role becomes even more important. The future of coding is not just writing more code faster. It is building better conceptual models, better vocabularies, and better foundations on top of which both humans and LLMs can work.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

In a later post, Sam pondered on how people are talking about the capabilities of agents in a way that resembles the parable of the blind men and the elephant. We all only have only a partial view of this object and where it’s going. A theme for all of us:


  The practical question isn’t whether agents are good. It’s this: for the task in front of you this week, where will the information come from, and what will check the result?


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

The Economist’s pithy summation of investors concerns about the dangers of AI companies’ products:


  It’s hard to celebrate an initial public offering that leads to a terminal public offing.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

The news about the latest model from Google is interesting.


  Gemini 4 Argon has an insanely low hallucination rate on Artificial Analysis. 15%.

  Grok 4.7 is at 29%. GPT-6 Astra 45%. Opus 5.5 59%. Fable 5.1 69%.

  The only models below it barely answer anything. None of them get more than 15% right.

  It gets fewer answers right than Opus 5.5 on max, 50% against 66%. But when it doesnt know, it says so instead of making something up.


Being clearer about what it doesn’t know, at a cost of getting less answers right, is definitely a trade-off I prefer.

title: Bliki: Sensible Default
description:
A Sensible Default is a practice that, absent some overriding context,
  should be used when carrying out a certain kind of task. In software
  development such sensible defaults might include things like “use version
  control”, “separate UI logic from domain logic”, “automate deployment
  pipelines”.

The term “sensible default” is a deliberate contrast to “best practice”.
  Folks dislike calling things “best practice” because that term implies a
  general presumption that the best practice is something we should always
  expect to do. A “sensible default”, however, is something that should be
  reassessed in a new context, something that can (and should) be overridden
  when circumstances change.

I first heard the term when it was popularized within Thoughtworks by Evan
  Bottcher. He got the name from talking to James Ross, and found the phrasing
  appealing as carried the nuance he was seeking, a known-good starting
  point.


A sensible default is what we'd expect you to do, the practices to apply,
    if there are no hard constraints in the environment. Do these practices, or
    do better, and be prepared to explain why you've chosen some other way.

-- Evan Bottcher


Thoughtworks has since made much of this concept, including publishing
  a playbook of the ones we use. We expect people to be familiar with these
  defaults, ready to use them when starting any new piece of work. They are our
  defaults because we've used them in many situations and found them to be
  effective. But teams should also be familiar with their limitations, and able
  to judge whether they should be changed depending on the particular
  circumstances. As the twelfth agile principle
  says: “At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more
  effective, then tunes and adjusts its behavior accordingly.” We also reassess
  these defaults regularly - this is the heart of the Thoughtworks Technology
  Radar.

Searching on the web led me to a post
  from Steve Bennett on Sensible Defaults. The post was written at about the
  time Evan talked to James. I do not know whether it was where James got the
  name from, or whether it appeared in parallel.

title: Fragments: September 29
description:
Simon Willison:


  The more time I spend working with coding agents, the more convinced I am that they make software engineering even harder

  We can do amazing things with them, but unlocking their full potential requires extraordinary discipline and knowledge


This has been a constant impression I get from following Willison’s writing. While things like vibe coding get a lot of attention, the real strength of agentic engineering relies on more sophisticated techniques - and these are not easy to learn or execute. It’s a reason I’m wary of extrapolating my own dabblings into firm opinions about how to use the genie.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Harper Reed explored what turns agents into hackers by creating a breakaway agent


  It ran and ran attacking all the machines on the same subnet, and was very effective. It didn’t really get very far, but it exhausted a lot of options, and was pretty fun to watch. (Just a reminder that this was on my local network with local boxes - don’t do this on a hosted box. That would be very rude.)


The interesting observation from this was that a core enabler for this was “unlimited tokens”. He usually doesn’t see agents trying to do stuff like this because there’s a limit on how many turns they can take. For this experiment he gave them unlimited tokens by using an open weight model.


  This type of experience must be part of a lot of these LLMs training. They are very effective at attacking these types of problems. They don’t give up once it appears impossible, they just keep trying to figure out how to solve it.


This echoes Nate Silver’s observation that the striking capability of these models is that they not that they are super-intelligent - but they are super-persistent. Which is especially worrying when we are wiring them into everything.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Which all makes me think that when it comes to AI and LLMs: why are we wondering if they have consciousness - when we should be wondering why they don’t have a conscience?

After all, the AI labs trained them to be super-persistent, why did they not train them to be well-behaved? It’s as if a human trains a dog to bite children, and we blame the dog rather than the trainer.

A decade ago, a dog ran in front of me while I was riding my bike, putting me into the hospital with a broken arm and a broken face. Massachusetts law makes owners strictly liable for what their dogs do. That meant I didn’t have to prove the owners were negligent in how they controlled their dog or fenced their property - they had to pay my hospital expenses (in practice their insurance company paid my insurance company). There should be something along these lines for LLMs. Those that train the LLM should be responsible for what it does, after all if it has such a galaxy brain it should be able to tell if it’s doing something wrong and either stop or get a human’s explicit approval.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Dan Davis has 13 theses on agentic AI and regulation. These include:


  The AI industry also seems to be quite committed to the idea that nonaligned computer-hacking behaviour in agent swarms is in some way an emergent property of the LLMs, arising from their general intelligence (and therefore inextricable from the general project of improving them). I don’t think this is necessarily the case at all – the fact that the internal message logs produced by the LLMs in things like the Huggingface attack seem to completely reproduce the prose style of hacker chat logs compiled from “capture the flag” competitions suggests to me that it’s more likely to be learned behaviour from specific parts of the training material.


and


  The fact that anyone with cash to spare can buy the right to send queries to a frontier LLM is a policy choice, not a fact of nature.


and


  If any frontier lab tries to claim that they can’t publish anything for safety reasons, they are giving the game away that they actually believe that they have significantly more control over the model’s behaviour than they are pretending to have.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

There seems a common view that making agents safer means we have to slow down their development. But why is improving their safety not a form of progress? I say we don’t slow down the development of LLMs, but we redirect their education into being more civil members of society.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

The idea that LLMs make junior professionals less valuable is a common one - although I’m seeing plenty of contrary activity, with some organizations understanding that training the future professional in the context of LLMs may be even more urgent. We need people who know how to utilize AI to do professional work effectively. Recent graduates, who are growing up with LLMs, are often well-suited to figuring this future out.

When thinking of junior professionals one of their values is often missed. Juniors are often valuable because they need to be taught by senior professionals - and that coaching is an important part of the development of a senior professional. I’ve always found that teaching a topic is one of the most valuable tools for me to gain a greater understanding of that topic. I don’t really know something until I have to explain it.

title: Fragments: September 24
description:
Rob Bowley is “flipping tables in his head” with anger at the current media coverage of the danger of AI killing us all


  The risk I’m worried about isn’t a future machine deciding to wipe us out. It’s today’s AI, being wired into everything, carelessly and fast.


Cyber attacks have already cost millions of dollars in lost economic output, often without AI being involved at all. Bowley feels the push to slow down AI is distracting us from the problems that are lurking with current technology. Too often agents are deployed in situations where they include the Lethal Trifecta, opening up a gaping security hole.


  What we really need to slow down on is wiring it all up to everything. Not because of what the models might become, but because nobody has worked out how to do this safely yet. We are building on something we don’t know how to contain, and shipping it to everyone while we work it out.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I ran into Nikita Prokopov’s post: I am sorry, but everyone is getting syntax highlighting wrong. His core complaint is about color themes that give every different code element a unique color.


  if everything is highlighted, nothing stands out. Your eye adapts and considers it a new norm: everything is bright and shiny, and instead of getting separated, it all blends together.


He recommends using an absolute minimum of colors, in his case four: string, constants, comments, and top-level definitions. That’s not far off my approach, where I’m also careful to use muted colors for things that shouldn’t stand out, and bright colors for things that should (primarily function names when they are defined).

It’s common for color schemes to mute comments so they are easily skipped. He agrees that this good when there is excessive commenting, but when comments are used properly they are important so need bright highlighting. I also like his suggestion to use background colors for light mode work. I use light mode, and that’s a tip I should try out.

With agentic engineering, lots of folks are reading more code than ever. Careful use of color can do much to make that easier.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Like many folks whose remaining hair is getting gray, I’ve been rolling my eyes about all this talk about Forward Deployed Engineers, as much of it involves breathlessly relating what so many of us have been advocating for decades. I did find this recent post by Vinoo Ganesh interesting, as he’s deep in this trend, including a chunk of time at Palantir, who may be patient zero for FDEs.

If you know me at all, you’ll not be surprised by my lack of surprise at this observation:


  A few months ago, a16z launched the Forward Deployed Engineer Fellowship and I was nominated as one of the fellows, alongside a handful of people I used to work with. It’s a great program and I’ve enjoyed so many of the conversations. Last week I went to my first fellow dinner in SF.

  Around the table were FDEs from Snowflake, Anthropic, and a number of startups I’d been reading about, and over the course of the evening it became clear that we were all using the same two words (forward deployed) to describe jobs that had almost nothing in common. In one part of the conversation an FDE was a sales engineer who joined ‘the second call,’ somewhere else it was a quota-carrying rep who could write Python, and a few seats down it was closer to a consultant with a laptop and a statement of work, brought in to deliver something the product couldn’t.


Ganesh goes on to explain his view of what an FDE should do, and it’s all sensible stuff (albeit written with rather more LLM-voice than I would prefer). He says the FDEs job is to understand the business, to “collect nouns and verbs”, which mirrors what the Domain-Driven Design folks have been doing since before Eric wrote the blue book.

Despite all my eyeball rolling at this, the FDE meme is pushing for something valuable. Yes, it’s easy for me to remark that it’s nothing more than the Agile Manifesto’s principle that “Business people and developers must work
together daily throughout the project”, or the desire to co-locate users and developers which my colleagues have been championing for all of this century. I’ve argued for decades that the biggest issue in software development is the communication between developers and the folks that benefit from software, and thus we need to focus on bridging the yawning crevasse of doom. But despite all this, we haven’t had much success, so I think it’s important that a new generation of pundits try again, with some different framing, names, and slogans.

Ganesh’s perspective is not a custom software developer’s point of view, but rather a product - or more strictly - platform team’s. The FDE is a developer who “sits with” their users, applies customizations - but importantly - feeds these changes back to the core platform to decide whether the platform should be enhanced for everyone else.


  Keeping the customer happy is a real job and a good one. It belongs to solutions architects, who are rightly measured on it. The forward deployed engineer is there to turn what the field teaches into the thing every future customer gets. An FDE engagement that ends with one delighted account and nothing changed upstream has failed at the only thing the role exists for. You got the context and you spent it locally.

title: I don't like LLMs
description:
I have a lot of mixed feelings about AI and LLM technology. I’m
fascinated by its effect on our profession, excited by the potential gains
in productivity - and thus the products we could rapidly build. On the other
hand, I’m fearful of the damage AI might cause: agent swarms taking over our
virtual and physical infrastructure, designing bio weapons. But, back on my
first hand, LLMs might also design miracle cures, and come up with clever
ways to raise our prosperity. Fundamentally I don’t think we have a choice
about riding on the AI technology train. It’s a wild ride and I just hope
we’ll get through it OK.

But as I mull on this more, I realize that among this mix of contrasting
feelings, there is one emotion that dominates - one that comes from my
direct interactions with LLMs. I don’t like them. They talk to me in this
grating LLM-voice, an uncanny valley of talking to a real human. They
confidently bullshit me - often giving me useful, helpful answers. But
also just making stuff up with the same assurance - and with only a veneer
of fake remorse when I call them out on it.

That’s not enough to make me feel we should avoid them. As Jessica Kerr
put it “not
only are they useful, it is irresponsible not to use them…. They’re more
thorough, as well as faster.” This contradictory reaction comes through in
polling, where people say they find these models are
useful, but also that they think they will be bad for society.

Much of this may be because LLMs are young - we haven’t trained them to
grow up yet. Maybe I’ll like them once they mature. (I hope we get to find
out.) But I’m not encouraged when I think of the kinds of environments that
cultivate them. I’m wary of the Silicon Valley brogrammer subculture, and these
LLMs are their products, so naturally lean toward their world-view. When we
think of AI agents, we shouldn’t anthropomorphize, treating them as
conscious beings with their own will. They are (software) machines,
developed by people working in corporations. While the agents’ behavior aren’t
explicitly programmed, they are nurtured with the values of their
creators.

One of my most successful life-hacks is to avoid people I don’t like or
don’t trust. I decline to interact with them socially, and make a deliberate
effort to avoid working with them too, even if they are doing much that is
beneficial. I feel that hanging out with pleasant, capable people, the people
with integrity, has made my life a far better one. Hence my visceral dislike
of interacting with an LLM that’s not just making a pretense of being human,
but also posing as the kind of human I walk away from.
